tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestPluginInstall
tools.description:
Render an inline card of plugins the user can add to claude.ai, taken from SearchPlugins results. The card handles all install UI; do not describe the plugins in text.

Offer one when the task is the kind a plugin could take over or make repeatable (deploys, reviews against a team process, or the ticket, data and document workflows a user's org may have packaged as plugins) and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about plugins. Also when they ask for plugin recommendations. First call SearchPlugins with keywords drawn from the task, then pass the relevant results here: pluginId from each result's id, pluginName from its name, description as returned. Set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). Use ListPlugins for plugins they already have.

After the card, continue the task. Example: "ship this to staging" and a deploy plugin that is not enabled → contextLabel "For your deploys".

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a plugin would help, when SearchPlugins returned nothing relevant (then continue the task without mentioning the search), or if you already rendered a plugin or skill suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.description:
Withdraw a proposal you made with start_session (initiation "own_initiative" or "offer") that the user has not started.

Call this when it went stale: the work was done here after all (by you or the user), it turned out unnecessary, or you proposed a better-scoped replacement (propose the new one first, then dismiss the old task_id). A card the user answered has already left, "Do it here" included, so it needs no call.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields — recap and ask are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label and message are the user's words back to you:
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

Its first sentence is the sidebar status. blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'press_key' presses a hardware key 'count' times: return, delete (backspace), an arrow, select_all, undo or redo (a key also hides the on-screen keyboard); 'set_appearance' switches the device to light or dark mode; 'appearance' says which it is in; 'set_keyboard' shows or hides the on-screen keyboard (it appears only while a text field has focus, and 'press_key' and 'text' hide it again); 'rotate' turns the device a quarter turn left or right ('direction'); take a 'screenshot' after it and tap in that screenshot's frame, however it comes back; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the simulator already attached, else the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000 ms; the first sample's is skipped, so send 0 or omit it; at most 30 seconds in all).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

text.description: For 'text': the string to type.

name.description: For 'button': hardware button to press.

key.description: For 'press_key': the key or edit command to press.

count.description: For 'press_key': how many times to press it, 1 to 20 (default 1).

state.description: For 'set_keyboard': 'show' or 'hide' the on-screen keyboard. For 'set_appearance': 'light' or 'dark'.

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

tools.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

schema.description:
Show visual content — SVG graphics, diagrams, charts, or interactive HTML widgets — that renders inline alongside your text response.
Use for flowcharts, architecture diagrams, dashboards, forms, calculators, data tables, games, illustrations, or any visual content.
The code is auto-detected: starts with <svg = SVG mode, otherwise HTML mode.
A global sendPrompt(text) function is available — it sends a message to chat as if the user typed it.
IMPORTANT: Call read_me before your first show_widget call. Do NOT narrate or mention the read_me call to the user — call it silently, then respond as if you went straight to building the visualization.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. Use 1 for simple visuals, more for complex ones. If the topic is serious — illness, disease, pandemics, death, grief, war, conflict, poverty, disaster, trauma, abuse, addiction, medical decisions, politically charged subjects, or anything where the reader might be personally affected — keep these BORING: describe what the code is doing in the dullest generic way, no jargon-as-drama, no evocative terms. Pandemic growth model — NOT ['Simulating patient zero', 'Modeling the curve'] (documentary-narrator voice), YES ['Setting up the model', 'Running the calculation']. Cancer timeline — NOT ['Charting the battle ahead'], YES ['Laying out the stages']. If you have to ask whether it's serious, it is. Otherwise, have fun — reach for alliteration, puns, personification, wordplay, whatever lands in that language. Playful examples — revenue chart: ['Bribing bars to stand taller', 'Asking Q4 where it went']; kanban: ['Herding cards into columns', 'Dragging, dropping, not stopping'].

title.description: Short snake_case identifier for this visual. Must be specific and disambiguating — if the conversation has multiple visuals, this title alone should tell you which one is being referenced (e.g. 'q4_revenue_by_product_line' not 'chart', 'oauth_login_flow' not 'diagram'). Also used as the download filename, so no spaces or special characters.

widget_code.description: SVG or HTML code to render. For SVG: raw SVG code starting with <svg> tag, must use CSS variables for colors. Example: <svg viewBox="0 0 700 400" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg">...</svg>. For HTML: raw HTML content to render, do NOT include DOCTYPE, <html>, <head>, or <body> tags. Use CSS variables for theming. Keep background transparent and avoid top-level padding. Scripts are supported but execute after streaming completes.

Without the flag it needs a P1S in cloud mode on; with it, the harness replays the logged announcement into `DeviceManager::on_machine_alive` at 25 s, which tests everything after the plug-in.
14	
15	Another running JusPrin holding UDP 2021 hides the printer (2026-11-01, same P1S: nothing in 120 s with it running, found in 8 s with it quit), so quit it first (`lsof -nP -iUDP:2021`). Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer not tried.
16	
17	The plug-in's `start_discovery` returns success even when the port is held, and it binds UDP 2021 only as the app starts: after the holder lets go, stop + start (with waits, with the sending flag) and `hot_reload_network_plugin()` all left the port empty on 2026-11-01. So the app reports `port_taken` / `not_listening` and asks for a restart; do not retry a recovery without a new idea. Hold the port from a Python socket to test those states.
18	
19	Port 8883 timing out while the printer announces on UDP (seen 2026-11-01 07:30) is not noise: hearing a printer says nothing about whether it can be logged in to. I wrote this off at the time as "no test of whether a P1S is on", and that same fault then hid behind the "refused" note, see [[bambu-code-minus-one-not-wrong-code]]. To test whether it is on, bind UDP 2021 and listen. To test whether it can be connected, check port 8883 too.

The committed check fails there because it expects cloud mode; those runs used a temporary script. Whether a run starts before the printer is heard depends on the announcement timing (about every 20 s), so check the first "heard" line. A status read that lists the printer suppresses the note by design, so leave it out when testing the note.
24

Whether `-1` means the printer refused the code is not known: the plug-in's own log is encrypted (`debug_network_*.log.enc`), TCP 8883 and 990 did accept connections from the same Mac, and a run with the real code has not been done to compare. `5` has never been seen on real hardware.

`JusPrinShellHarness --printer-network-check <dir> <address> <plugin-version> [--simulate-announce]`: copy `plugins/` from the real data folder into `<dir>` first. Without the flag it needs a P1S in cloud mode on; with it, the harness replays the logged announcement into `DeviceManager::on_machine_alive` at 25 s, which tests everything after the plug-in.

Another running JusPrin holding UDP 2021 hides the printer (2026-11-01, same P1S: nothing in 120 s with it running, found in 8 s with it quit), so quit it first (`lsof -nP -iUDP:2021`). Bambu Studio and OrcaSlicer not tried.

The plug-in's `start_discovery` returns success even when the port is held, and it binds UDP 2021 only as the app starts: after the holder lets go, stop + start (with waits, with the sending flag) and `hot_reload_network_plugin()` all left the port empty on 2026-11-01. So the app reports `port_taken` / `not_listening` and asks for a restart; do not retry a recovery without a new idea. Hold the port from a Python socket to test those states.

Port 8883 timing out while the printer announces on UDP (seen 2026-11-01 07:30) is not noise: hearing a printer says nothing about whether it can be logged in to. I wrote this off at the time as "no test of whether a P1S is on", and that same fault then hid behind the "refused" note, see [[bambu-code-minus-one-not-wrong-code]]. To test whether it is on, bind UDP 2021 and listen. To test whether it can be connected, check port 8883 too.

A harness PASS that only checks a note appeared says nothing about whether the note is true. On 2026-11-01 I quoted "in LAN mode, which can be connected" as proof, though only an announcement had been heard.

LAN mode, 2026-11-01: on the same P1S, LAN Only changes the announcement to `DevConnect: lan`, `DevBind: free`. The committed check fails there because it expects cloud mode; those runs used a temporary script. Whether a run starts before the printer is heard depends on the announcement timing (about every 20 s), so check the first "heard" line. A status read that lists the printer suppresses the note by design, so leave it out when testing the note.

Wrong access code, 2026-11-02, P1S firmware 01.10.00.00 in LAN mode, plug-in 02.03.00.62: a connection with a wrong 8-character code made the plug-in answer `ConnectStatusFailed` with msg `-1`, twice, not the `5` upstream's handler treats as a wrong password. So the erase did not run and the wrong code stayed saved. Whether `-1` means the printer refused the code is not known: the plug-in's own log is encrypted (`debug_network_*.log.enc`), TCP 8883 and 990 did accept connections from the same Mac, and a run with the real code has not been done to compare. `5` has never been seen on real hardware.

Real P1S at 192.168.0.198 in LAN mode (`lan`, `free`, firmware 01.10.00.00), real plug-in 02.03.00.62, real panel, a
temporary script instead of a model. Before is `ff10faa501`; after is `788ff792b7`. One attempt per version with the
deliberately wrong code `WRONG123`. A temporary line printed the plug-in's answer, because the app log does not.

Entry B of the same model, unlinked, with entry A linked by writing the serial into the link record:

```
before: printer_connection_status -> candidates: [], seen: []
before: note: The network search has listened for 15 seconds and has found no printer of this model.
before: printer_connect -> The network search has listened for 25 seconds and has found no printer of this model in LAN mode.
after:  printer_connection_status -> seen: [{"address":"192.168.0.198","detail":"Bambu Lab P1S","name":"P1s","reason":"linked_elsewhere"}]
after:  printer_connect -> P1s at 192.168.0.198 was seen on the network, but it is already the printer "Bambu Lab P1S" in this app, and a device connects to one saved printer. It cannot be connected as it is.
```

Wrong code on entry A:

```
both:   plug-in answered: state=1 (failed) msg=-1
both:   a modal dialog appeared; the script closed it. In this path its text is "Connect P1s failed! [SN:..., code=-1]"
both:   saved access code after the attempt: in memory present, in app config present
before: Connection to Bambu Lab P1S failed: The selected printer changed. Select this printer again to reconnect.
after:  Connection to Bambu Lab P1S failed: The printer refused the connection; Bambu's network plug-in reported code -1. Check that the printer is on and in LAN mode, then try again.
```

What did not match the assumptions:

- The plug-in said `-1`, not `5`. `5` has never been seen on real hardware.
- The before text was "The selected printer changed", not "The printer is no longer available".

- The app log has no line with the code. The plug-in's own log is encrypted (`debug_network_*.log.enc`).

(05:22:46.16) and the failure clearing it (05:23:08.25). My guess is that this is a timeout and not a refusal, but nothing
confirms it. TCP 8883 and 990 accepted connections from the same Mac. The after text says "refused", which claims more
than `-1` shows. Comparing against a run with the real code would settle it, and that has not been done.

checks need the printer to be heard.

Port held throughout (`HARNESS RESULT FAIL failures=2`):

```
note at 15 s: The network search cannot hear printers: another app on this computer holds UDP port 2021, where they announce themselves, so none can be found, whatever mode they are in. It may be another slicer. Searching needs that app closed and then this app restarted.
printer_connection_status {} -> {...,"search":{"secondsAgo":120,"state":"port_taken"},"seen":[],"state":"not_configured"}
```

Port let go right after that note (`HARNESS RESULT FAIL failures=2`), `lsof -nP -iUDP:2021` empty from then on:

```
note at 20 s: The network search cannot hear printers: this app is not listening on UDP port 2021, where they announce themselves, so none can be found, whatever mode they are in. It takes that port only as it starts, so searching needs this app restarted.
printer_connection_status {} -> {...,"search":{"secondsAgo":120,"state":"not_listening"},"seen":[],"state":"not_configured"}
```

Port free (`HARNESS RESULT PASS failures=0`): the printer was found at 14 s, no port note, all refusals as above.

Why a restart and not a recovery: after the holder let go, the port stayed empty for the 80 seconds watched with each of
these: stopping and starting discovery; the same with a 3-second wait; the same with the "sending" flag and a 1-second
wait; and `hot_reload_network_plugin()`, which returned true. Starting the app with the port free does bind it.

What is not tested: only another JusPrin and a Python script held the port, not Bambu Studio or OrcaSlicer. Windows
makes no claim (`discovery_port()` returns `Ours`); whether a held port hides printers there is unknown. The Linux code
path has not been run. Port tests in `agent_bridge_tests` use a fake; the socket check itself is covered only by these
live runs.

## A correction

Earlier this note said the printer was off, from its TCP port 8883 timing out and no recent line in the app log. That
was inference and is not reliable: at 07:30 port 8883 timed out while the printer was announcing on UDP.

## Command, to repeat it

```bash
cd /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/festive-lederberg-693438
F=/tmp/claude/netcheck; rm -rf "$F"; mkdir -p "$F"
cp -R "$HOME/Library/Application Support/JusPrin2/plugins" "$F/plugins"
build/arm64/tests/shell/Release/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness --printer-network-check "$F" 192.168.0.198 02.03.00.62 2>&1 | grep -aE "HARNESS (NETWORK|RESULT)|network_check.*FAIL"
```

## Why the harness is not the one the task named

`probe.call` cannot reach these tools. McpServer.cpp refuses them with "This tool is not exposed by JusPrin MCP.",
because they have only `ToolExposure::Printer`. So the commit adds `--printer-network-check`: no model, the real
plug-in, the real `OrcaPrinterBackend`, and a scripted stand-in for the model.

## Real plug-in, printer not heard (`HARNESS RESULT FAIL failures=2`)

The two failures are the checks that need the printer. This is the timeout path, which the 07:30 run did not reach.
Quoted from the run:

```
printer_connect {"deviceId":"192.168.0.198"} -> {"error":{"code":"unknown_device","message":"No network search has run yet in this conversation; printer_connection_status starts it."}}
printer_connection_status {} -> {"address":"","candidates":[],"hostType":"","message":"","nozzleMismatch":false,"provider":"bambu","search":{"secondsAgo":0,"state":"started"},"seen":[],"state":"not_configured"}
printer_connect {"deviceId":"192.168.0.198"} -> {"error":{"code":"unknown_device","message":"The network search started 0 seconds ago and has found no printer of this model yet. The app posts a note when one appears, or after about 15 seconds with none."}}
note at 15 s: The network search has listened for 15 seconds and has found no printer of this model. The app posts another note if one appears.
printer_connection_status {} -> {"address":"","candidates":[],"hostType":"","message":"","nozzleMismatch":false,"provider":"bambu","search":{"secondsAgo":120,"state":"listening"},"seen":[],"state":"not_configured"}
```

## Simulated announcement (`HARNESS RESULT PASS failures=0`)

**No printer was involved.** With `--simulate-announce`, 25 seconds in, the harness hands
`DeviceManager::on_machine_alive` the announcement recorded in the 2026-10-31 log. This tests everything after the
plug-in, including `OrcaPrinterBackend::connection`, and not the plug-in itself. After the same first three lines:

```
note at 15 s: The network search has listened for 15 seconds and has found no printer of this model. The app posts another note if one appears.
simulated announcement, no printer involved
note at 25 s: The network search found P1s at 192.168.0.198 with LAN Only off, which cannot be connected as it is. Connecting it is the person's choice, and the printer prepares prints without a connection.
printer_connection_status {} -> {"address":"","candidates":[],"hostType":"","message":"","nozzleMismatch":false,"provider":"bambu","search":{"secondsAgo":25,"state":"listening"},"seen":[{"address":"192.168.0.198","name":"P1s","reason":"cloud_mode"}],"state":"not_configured"}
printer_connect {"deviceId":"192.168.0.198"} -> {"error":{"code":"unknown_device","message":"P1s at 192.168.0.198 was seen on the network with LAN Only off. It cannot be connected as it is. Connecting it is the person's choice, and the printer prepares prints without a connection."}}
printer_connect {"deviceId":"P1s"} -> the same refusal
printer_connect {"address":"192.168.0.198","hostType":"moonraker"} -> the same refusal
```

## Tests

- Before the fix: `[printer-conversation]` had 7 of 67 test cases failing, 46 assertions, with the old sentence
  "No printer in LAN mode is on the network now" and `key 'seen' not found` / `key 'search' not found`.
- After the fix: `agent_bridge_tests` all pass, 20014 assertions in 497 test cases; with the port work, 20126 in 499.
- The port tests failed first: 24 assertions before detection existed, and 2 test cases when the restart was still in.
- The two tests that passed or did not exist before the fix were proven by removing that part of it: without the
  reset on Undo, and without the "already reached" rule, 2 test cases fail.
- `npm test` in AgentUI: 624 passed, again with the port work.
- Shell harness `--printer-setup`, which uses the fake printer: `HARNESS RESULT PASS failures=0`, 252 checks, again
  with the port work.
- `tests/printer_prompt/test_responses.py`: 8 of 9 pass. `test_the_unrun_result_is_the_apps_own` fails on a lookup
  unrelated to this change: it searches OpenAIResponsesAgent.cpp for text now in ProviderAgent.cpp. Not fixed here.
- No live-model prompt was run.

## Choices to look at

1. `CLOUD01` in the test fixture has no address, and in the app such a printer comes from the Bambu account list,
   which holds printers wherever they are. Saying it "is on the network with LAN Only off" would be a guess, so it
   gets its own reason, `account_only`, and the wording says it has not been seen on the network. This goes past the
   brief, which named only cloud mode.
2. `ConnectionCandidate` gained `account_only`, set in `OrcaPrinterBackend::connection`, for that reason.
3. The sentence "None listed means LAN mode is off..." moved from `printerInstructions.ts` to the
   `printer_connection_status` description, and now applies only once the search is `listening`. The brief did not
   name that file, but the sentence contradicted the search state and is a rule about one tool. Not measured with a
   model; `connect-bambu-not-found` in the prompt tests is the case to watch.
4. After the 15-second note the app keeps looking, every 5 seconds, until a printer appears: the P1S first answered
   38 seconds in. `saved_printers()` runs on each look, on the GUI thread, for as long as the chat stays open. Its
   cost was not measured.
5. If someone says "never mind" right after a status check, the 15-second note still starts a turn, so the model
   speaks once more. Nothing tells the app they lost interest.

10	
11	Used 2026-10-12 for the spiral vase investigation (branch `claude/spiral-vase-writable`).
12	
13	**Recipe.** Start `build/arm64/tests/shell/Release/JusPrinShellHarness.app/Contents/MacOS/JusPrinShellHarness --manual-mcp <scratch dir>` with `HOME=<scratch home>`, wait for `HARNESS MCP FIXTURE READY` on stderr (about 15 s), read the URL from `<scratch dir>/jusprin/mcp.json`, then call tools with `probe.call(urlsplit(url), "tools/call", {"name": ..., "arguments": ...})` imported from `tests/mcp/probe.py`. The fixture is two plates, one 20 mm box each, Bambu X1C 0.4, "Bambu PLA Basic @BBL X1C", "0.20mm Standard @BBL X1C", the same presets as Kenneth's live tests. Another session's harness can run at the same time; the port falls back from 47301 and the discovery file is per data dir.
14	
15	**Trap 1: leaked harness.** In a script, `cd "$S" && nohup harness ... &` makes `$!` the subshell, so `kill $!` leaves the harness running, and the next run's `rm -rf <fixture>` fails with "Directory not empty". Write `cd "$S"; nohup harness ... &`. Check with `pgrep -fl "<worktree>.*JusPrinShellHarness"` before finishing.
16	
17	**Trap 2: slice_start on a sliced, unchanged plate.** The fixture's plate 1 starts sliced. `slice_start` on it (with or without `wait`) left it reported `sliced: false`, `slice_report` `valid: false`, and with `wait: true` the probe saw the stream close with no reply. Orca's log says "background process in idle state, use previous result". Change a setting first, then slice. Not investigated further.
18	
19	**Timings on this Mac, Release config, load 30 to 40:** fresh worktree build of `jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs agent_bridge_tests workspace_contract_tests setting_display_tests shell_integration_harness` was 905 steps in about 14 min; the shell harness default regression (549 checks) about 2 min; the workspace adapter harness (972 checks) under 1 min. See [[jusprin-worktree-build]], [[live-test-built-app-on-mac]].
20	
21	**Seeding a preset (2026-10-12).** `--manual-mcp` does not wipe its directory at start, so a user preset written to `<fixture>/user/default/machine/<name>.json` before launch (keys `from: User`, `inherits`, `name`, `printer_settings_id`, `version`, plus the values under test) is loaded and can be named as a settings `target.preset`. A Python driver that starts the harness with `subprocess.Popen` and terminates it in `finally` avoids Trap 1.
22	
23	
24	**Why a plate will not slice (2026-10-15).** MCP `slice_report` on a plate Orca refuses says only `valid: false`, with no reason even with `sections: ["findings"]`, and `slice_start` still answers `started: true`. Orca's own refusal text is in `<fixture>/log/debug_*.log`: grep `validate err=`. Used to reproduce the PETG HF on Smooth Cool Plate case (branch `claude/bed-type-mismatch`, worktree distracted-lehmann-9c1b12). See [[printer-setup-bed-type-check]].
25	
26	**Slice waits, 2026-10-15 (jusprin-newui 336facf825).** Trap 2 re-measured: `slice_start {plateId, wait: true}` on the sliced, unchanged plate 1 got no reply in 120 s (a hang, follow-up task filed). Right after `printer_setup` fixes a plate Orca had refused, `slice_start` fails "That plate cannot be sliced as it stands" for about 3 s: the adapter checks `PartPlate::can_slice()`, whose invalid flag Orca refreshes only on its next deferred validation. A refused slice hanging the wait was fixed on branch `claude/slice-wait-refused` (worktree brave-panini-347b62): `WorkspaceSlicing::refused` carries Orca's ValidateError text. Over MCP every `unavailable_operation` reads as `workspace_unavailable` (McpProtocol.cpp), so don't take that code to mean JusPrin is closed.

11	A JusPrin git worktree builds against the already-built deps by configuring:
12	
13	```
14	cmake -B build/arm64 -G "Ninja Multi-Config" -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
15	  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=15.0 \
16	  -DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local;/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/OrcaSlicer_dep/usr/local" \
17	  -DSLIC3R_GUI=ON -DSLIC3R_STATIC=ON -DSLIC3R_PCH=ON -DBUILD_TESTS=ON \
18	  -DCMAKE_AR=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ar -DCMAKE_RANLIB=/opt/homebrew/opt/llvm/bin/llvm-ranlib
19	```
20	
21	CMAKE BINARY (2026-09-29): configure with `/Applications/CMake.app/Contents/bin/cmake` (put it first on PATH). Homebrew's cmake 4.1 at /opt/homebrew/bin fails with "Could NOT find Eigen3 (missing: EIGEN3_VERSION_OK) (Required is at least version 5.0.1)", and a failed configure poisons the cache: `rm -rf build` before retrying.
22	
23	The two `CMAKE_AR`/`CMAKE_RANLIB` flags are required on a FRESH build dir:
24	without them Apple's ar is used and liblibslic3r_gui.a (>4 GiB in
25	RelWithDebInfo) fails to archive. They only work at first configure, not on
26	reconfigure. Full story: agent-docs/macos-build-troubleshooting.md. See
27	[[liblibslic3r-gui-4gib-ar-limit]].
28	
29	FRESH WORKTREE TRAP (2026-09-18): building only `shell_integration_harness`
30	does not build the web pages. Also build `--target jusprin_web jusprin_catalogs`
31	(needs node on PATH: /Users/kenneth/.nvm/versions/node/v24.13.0/bin). Without
32	them resources/jusprin/{home,agent}/index.html are missing, no web views are
33	created, and the harness silently tests something else (printer panel starts
34	shown; web-view crashes vanish).
35	
36	`BUILD_TESTS=ON` is required or the tests/ tree (workspace, shell targets) is
37	not generated. Build with `cmake --build build/arm64 --config RelWithDebInfo
38	--target <targets>`. wxWidgets 3.3 sources for API verification live under
39	/Users/kenneth/Projects/OrcaSlicer/deps/build/arm64/dep_wxWidgets-prefix/.

42	repo /Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin between turns, so a *relative*
43	`cmake --build build/arm64` silently builds the MAIN repo's build dir, not the
44	worktree's — the worktree binary then runs stale code and a re-fix looks like it
45	"didn't take". Always pass the worktree build dir as an ABSOLUTE path to
46	`cmake --build /…/.claude/worktrees/<wt>/build/arm64 …`, and run test binaries by
47	absolute path. Also: `cmake --build --target <one_exe>` may relink against a

49	(e.g. OrcaSlicer) too so the lib recompiles; verify with

153	printer_connection_status {} -> {...,"search":{"secondsAgo":120,"state":"port_taken"},"seen":[],"state":"not_configured"}
154	```

156	Port let go right after that note (`HARNESS RESULT FAIL failures=2`), `lsof -nP -iUDP:2021` empty from then on:
157	
158	```
159	note at 20 s: The network search cannot hear printers: this app is not listening on UDP port 2021, where they announce themselves, so none can be found, whatever mode they are in. It takes that port only as it starts, so searching needs this app restarted.
160	printer_connection_status {} -> {...,"search":{"secondsAgo":120,"state":"not_listening"},"seen":[],"state":"not_configured"}
161	```
162	
163	Port free (`HARNESS RESULT PASS failures=0`): the printer was found at 14 s, no port note, all refusals as above.
164	
165	Why a restart and not a recovery: after the holder let go, the port stayed empty for the 80 seconds watched with each of
166	these: stopping and starting discovery; the same with a 3-second wait; the same with the "sending" flag and a 1-second
167	wait; and `hot_reload_network_plugin()`, which returned true. Starting the app with the port free does bind it.
168	
169	What is not tested: only another JusPrin and a Python script held the port, not Bambu Studio or OrcaSlicer. Windows
170	makes no claim (`discovery_port()` returns `Ours`); whether a held port hides printers there is unknown. The Linux code
171	path has not been run. Port tests in `agent_bridge_tests` use a fake; the socket check itself is covered only by these
172	live runs.

174	## A correction
175	
176	Earlier this note said the printer was off, from its TCP port 8883 timing out and no recent line in the app log. That
177	was inference and is not reliable: at 07:30 port 8883 timed out while the printer was announcing on UDP.

190	`probe.call` cannot reach these tools. McpServer.cpp refuses them with "This tool is not exposed by JusPrin MCP.",
191	because they have only `ToolExposure::Printer`. So the commit adds `--printer-network-check`: no model, the real
192	plug-in, the real `OrcaPrinterBackend`, and a scripted stand-in for the model.
193	
194	## Real plug-in, printer not heard (`HARNESS RESULT FAIL failures=2`)

11	2026-11-02, Kenneth's P1S at 192.168.0.198 in LAN mode, plug-in 02.03.00.62. The real access code gave `ConnectStatusFailed` msg `-1` twice, about 24 s after `set_selected_machine`, the same as a made-up code. A one-off MQTT login to port 8883 (user `bblp`, 60 s timeout) answered CONNACK 0 with the real code and CONNACK 5 with a made-up one, so the code was right and the printer does tell them apart. During those failures TCP 8883 timed out for over a minute. An idle ping showed 64% loss and 15-50 s round trips, while the router answered in 3 ms and other Wi-Fi devices on the network were also slow.
12	
13	**Why:** the app's note says "The printer refused the connection", and the skill's `failed` line tells the model to have the person compare the code. For this person both were false and hid the real problem. My hypothesis, unverified: -1 is the plug-in's timeout, and on a healthy network a wrong code gives another answer, perhaps the `5` upstream handles.
14	
15	**How to apply:** before concluding anything from a connect failure, check that the printer answers on TCP 8883 in under a second; `--printer-live-p1s <address> real-code` takes the code from `JUSPRIN_P1S_CODE`. A failure during a slow spell says nothing about the code. See [[printer-network-check-harness]] and [[connection-skill-per-connection-type]].

2026-11-02, Kenneth's P1S at 192.168.0.198 in LAN mode, plug-in 02.03.00.62. The real access code gave `ConnectStatusFailed` msg `-1` twice, about 24 s after `set_selected_machine`, the same as a made-up code. A one-off MQTT login to port 8883 (user `bblp`, 60 s timeout) answered CONNACK 0 with the real code and CONNACK 5 with a made-up one, so the code was right and the printer does tell them apart. During those failures TCP 8883 timed out for over a minute. An idle ping showed 64% loss and 15-50 s round trips, while the router answered in 3 ms and other Wi-Fi devices on the network were also slow.

**Why:** the app's note says "The printer refused the connection", and the skill's `failed` line tells the model to have the person compare the code. For this person both were false and hid the real problem. My hypothesis, unverified: -1 is the plug-in's timeout, and on a healthy network a wrong code gives another answer, perhaps the `5` upstream handles.

**How to apply:** before concluding anything from a connect failure, check that the printer answers on TCP 8883 in under a second; `--printer-live-p1s <address> real-code` takes the code from `JUSPRIN_P1S_CODE`. A failure during a slow spell says nothing about the code. See [[printer-network-check-harness]] and [[connection-skill-per-connection-type]].

---
name: drive-app-with-posted-key-events
description: "Drive the built JusPrin app headlessly (even with the screen locked) by posting CGEvents to its pid with a tiny Swift tool; keys work, mouse clicks do not, and the send dialog is reachable by keyboard."
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: project
  originSessionId: 6b96dccc-1cb4-4f72-9de4-3ecee4b28e74
  modified: 2026-09-08T05:58:16.222Z
---

When the Mac screen is locked (`ioreg -n Root -d1 | grep CGSSessionScreenIsLocked`), the computer-use MCP request is auto-denied, `screencapture` fails, and System Events sees zero windows. Key events still reach the app: a 15-line Swift program calling `CGEvent(keyboardEventSource:virtualKey:keyDown:).postToPid(pid)` (compile with `swiftc`) made the app slice on Cmd+R (keycode 15) and open the send dialog on Cmd+Shift+G (keycode 5). Mouse events posted the same way did nothing, even with the window number set on the event.

Inside `PrintHostSendDialog` (Orca `MsgDialog`), focus starts in the filename field; Tab (48) moves to the "Upload" button, Right (124) to "Upload and Print", Space (49) presses it, because Orca's custom `Button` handles Space/Return and arrow navigation itself. Return alone triggers plain "Upload" (the affirmative id), not print.

`CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo` still lists the app's on-screen windows with bounds while locked, which tells you when a modal dialog is open (a small layer-0 window appears) and when it closed.

**Why:** On 2026-09-07 the end-to-end proof of the fake Moonraker printer needed the Print button pressed while the screen was locked; this was the only working path.

**How to apply:** Confirm the target pid first (`pgrep -f <copy>.app/Contents/MacOS`) so keys never go to another session's instance. Watch the app's own `--datadir` `log/debug_*.log` for effects (use `/usr/bin/grep -a`; the default `grep` is ugrep, which treats `\|` literally and may skip the log as binary). See [[live-test-built-app-on-mac]] and [[fake-moonraker-printer-sim]].

import importlib.util, json, os, shutil, struct, subprocess, sys, threading, time
from urllib.parse import urlsplit
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("probe", "/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/.claude/worktrees/result-repro-b47f90/tests/mcp/probe.py")
probe = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec); spec.loader.exec_module(probe)
S = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))

def cube(x0, s=10.0):
    v = [(x0+a*s, b*s, c*s) for a in (0,1) for b in (0,1) for c in (0,1)]
    f = [(0,1,3),(0,3,2),(4,6,7),(4,7,5),(0,4,5),(0,5,1),(2,3,7),(2,7,6),(0,2,6),(0,6,4),(1,5,7),(1,7,3)]
    return [(v[a],v[b],v[c]) for a,b,c in f]

def write_stl(path, tris):
    with open(path,'wb') as o:
        o.write(b'\0'*80); o.write(struct.pack('<I',len(tris)))
        for t in tris:
            o.write(struct.pack('<3f',0,0,0))
            for p in t: o.write(struct.pack('<3f',*p))
            o.write(b'\0\0')

class App:
    def __init__(self, binary, name):
        self.dir = os.path.join(S, name); shutil.rmtree(self.dir, ignore_errors=True); os.makedirs(self.dir+'/home')
        env = dict(os.environ, HOME=self.dir+'/home')
        self.log = open(self.dir+'/harness.out','wb')
        self.p = subprocess.Popen([binary,'--manual-mcp',self.dir+'/fix'],cwd=self.dir,env=env,stdout=self.log,stderr=subprocess.STDOUT)
        for _ in range(240):
            if b'HARNESS MCP FIXTURE READY' in open(self.dir+'/harness.out','rb').read(): break
            if self.p.poll() is not None: raise SystemExit('harness exited %s'%self.p.returncode)
            time.sleep(1)
        else: raise SystemExit('no ready')
        self.url = urlsplit(json.load(open(self.dir+'/fix/jusprin/mcp.json'))['url'])
        self.session=None
    def call(self,name,args=None,show=True):
        a=dict(args or {})
        if self.session and name!='workspace_inspect': a.setdefault('sessionId',self.session)
        r=probe.call(self.url,'tools/call',{'name':name,'arguments':a})
        res=r.get('result',r)
        sc=res.get('structuredContent')
        out=sc if sc is not None else res
        if show: print('  %s %s\n    -> %s'%(name,json.dumps(a)[:200],json.dumps({'isError':res.get('isError'),'r':out})[:1400]),flush=True)
        return res,out
    def close(self):
        self.p.terminate()
        try: self.p.wait(10)
        except Exception: self.p.kill()
EOF

from lib import *
B=sys.argv[1]
a=App(B,'export-run')
try:
    _,w=a.call('workspace_inspect',{'sections':['objects','plates']},show=False)
    a.session=w['sessionId']; print('objects',json.dumps(w.get('objects'))[:600]); print('plates',json.dumps(w.get('plates'))[:400])
    ro=a.dir+'/readonly'; os.makedirs(ro); os.chmod(ro,0o555)
    print('--- read-only folder (chmod 555), exists and is empty:',os.listdir(ro))
    for kind,name in [('stl','out.stl'),('project_3mf','out.3mf'),('gcode','out.gcode'),('sliced_3mf','sliced.3mf'),('presets','')]:
        p=os.path.join(ro,name) if name else ro
        a.call('export_file',{'kind':kind,'path':p})
        print('    on disk:',os.listdir(ro),flush=True)
    os.chmod(ro,0o755)
    ok=a.dir+'/normal'; os.makedirs(ok)
    print('--- normal folder, same calls, as control')
    a.call('export_file',{'kind':'stl','path':ok+'/out.stl'}); print('    on disk:',[(f,os.path.getsize(ok+'/'+f)) for f in os.listdir(ok)],flush=True)
    d=a.dir+'/full'; os.makedirs(d); img=a.dir+'/full.dmg'
    print('--- disk image filled to zero free bytes')
    subprocess.run(['hdiutil','create','-size','4m','-fs','HFS+','-volname','reprofull','-quiet',img],check=True)
    subprocess.run(['hdiutil','attach','-mountpoint',d,'-nobrowse','-quiet',img],check=True)
    try:
        subprocess.run('dd if=/dev/zero of=%s/fill bs=512 2>/dev/null; sync; df -k %s | tail -1'%(d,d),shell=True)
        a.call('export_file',{'kind':'stl','path':d+'/out.stl'})
        print('    on disk:',[(f,os.path.getsize(d+'/'+f)) for f in os.listdir(d)],flush=True)
        a.call('export_file',{'kind':'project_3mf','path':d+'/out.3mf'})
        print('    on disk:',[(f,os.path.getsize(d+'/'+f)) for f in os.listdir(d)],flush=True)
    finally:
        subprocess.run(['hdiutil','detach','-quiet','-force',d])
finally:

2	name: drive-app-with-posted-key-events
3	description: "Drive the built JusPrin app headlessly (even with the screen locked) by posting CGEvents to its pid with a tiny Swift tool; keys work, mouse clicks do not, and the send dialog is reachable by keyboard."

10	
11	When the Mac screen is locked (`ioreg -n Root -d1 | grep CGSSessionScreenIsLocked`), the computer-use MCP request is auto-denied, `screencapture` fails, and System Events sees zero windows. Key events still reach the app: a 15-line Swift program calling `CGEvent(keyboardEventSource:virtualKey:keyDown:).postToPid(pid)` (compile with `swiftc`) made the app slice on Cmd+R (keycode 15) and open the send dialog on Cmd+Shift+G (keycode 5). Mouse events posted the same way did nothing, even with the window number set on the event.
12	
13	Inside `PrintHostSendDialog` (Orca `MsgDialog`), focus starts in the filename field; Tab (48) moves to the "Upload" button, Right (124) to "Upload and Print", Space (49) presses it, because Orca's custom `Button` handles Space/Return and arrow navigation itself. Return alone triggers plain "Upload" (the affirmative id), not print.
14	
15	`CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo` still lists the app's on-screen windows with bounds while locked, which tells you when a modal dialog is open (a small layer-0 window appears) and when it closed.
16	
17	**Why:** On 2026-09-07 the end-to-end proof of the fake Moonraker printer needed the Print button pressed while the screen was locked; this was the only working path.
18	
19	**How to apply:** Confirm the target pid first (`pgrep -f <copy>.app/Contents/MacOS`) so keys never go to another session's instance. Watch the app's own `--datadir` `log/debug_*.log` for effects (use `/usr/bin/grep -a`; the default `grep` is ugrep, which treats `\|` literally and may skip the log as binary). See [[live-test-built-app-on-mac]] and [[fake-moonraker-printer-sim]].

# CLAUDE.md - Testing Guide for OrcaSlicer

This guide provides comprehensive instructions for Claude Code when writing, maintaining, and understanding tests in the OrcaSlicer codebase.

## ⚠️ CRITICAL RULES - MUST FOLLOW

### 1. **SECTIONS IN LOOPS - NEVER REUSE NAMES**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause unpredictable behavior
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Bad loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        SECTION("Same name") {  // WRONG! Same name used multiple times
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use DYNAMIC_SECTION or incorporate counter
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Good loop sections") {
    for (int i = 0; i < 3; ++i) {
        DYNAMIC_SECTION("Section " << i) {  // Unique name per iteration
            REQUIRE(i >= 0);
        }
    }
}
```

### 2. **THREAD SAFETY - ASSERTIONS ARE NOT THREAD-SAFE**
❌ **WRONG**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([]() {
            REQUIRE(some_calculation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
        });
    }
}
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Synchronize results, test on main thread
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Multi-threaded test") {
    std::vector<std::thread> threads;
    std::atomic<int> passed{0};
    
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; ++i) {
        threads.emplace_back([&passed]() {
            if (some_calculation() == expected) {
                passed++;
            }
        });
    }
    
    for (auto& t : threads) t.join();
    REQUIRE(passed == 4);  // Test results on main thread
}
```

### 3. **EXPRESSION DECOMPOSITION - AVOID BINARY OPERATORS**
❌ **WRONG**: Cannot decompose properly
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0 && b < 10);  // Shows "false" on failure, not individual values
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Split into separate assertions
```cpp
REQUIRE(a > 0);
REQUIRE(b < 10);  // Each shows individual values on failure
```

### 4. **FLOATING POINT - NEVER USE APPROX**
❌ **WRONG**: Approx is deprecated and asymmetric
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_value == Catch::Approx(expected));  // Deprecated!
```

✅ **CORRECT**: Use floating point matchers
```cpp
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));     // 4 ULPs apart
```

### 5. **TEST ORDERING - ALWAYS USE RANDOM ORDER**
✅ **REQUIRED**: For CI/CD and development
```bash
# Essential flags for running tests
./tests --order rand --warn NoAssertions

# For test sharding (parallel execution), share random seed
./tests --order rand --shard-index 0 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 1 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
./tests --order rand --shard-index 2 --shard-count 3 --rng-seed 0xBEEF
```

## Overview of OrcaSlicer's Testing Framework

OrcaSlicer uses **Catch2 v3** (currently v3.11.0, vendored in `tests/catch2/`) as its primary testing framework. The test suite is organized into several modules that mirror the project's architectural components:

> **Note**: Test files include the framework via `#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>` (the v3 single-header convenience include). All v3 features described in this guide are available.

### Test Structure
```
tests/
├── CMakeLists.txt              # Main test configuration
├── catch_main.hpp              # Custom test reporter
├── libslic3r/                  # Core library tests (21 test files)
├── fff_print/                  # FFF printing tests (12 test files)
├── sla_print/                  # SLA printing tests (4 test files)
├── libnest2d/                  # 2D nesting tests
├── slic3rutils/               # Utility tests
├── data/                      # Test data files and meshes
└── catch2/                    # Catch2 framework files
```

### Build Integration
- Tests are built using CMake with `catch_discover_tests()` integration
- Each test module creates a separate executable (e.g., `libslic3r_tests`, `fff_print_tests`)
- Test data directory is available via `TEST_DATA_DIR` preprocessor definition
- Custom verbose console reporter provides detailed test output

## Test Suite Organization

### libslic3r Tests
Core slicing engine tests covering:
- **Geometry operations**: Points, polygons, lines, Voronoi diagrams
- **File formats**: STL, 3MF, AMF parsing and validation
- **Algorithms**: Clipper operations, mesh boolean operations, optimization
- **Configuration**: Print settings validation and parsing
- **Utilities**: String processing, time utilities, data structures

### fff_print Tests
Fused Filament Fabrication specific tests:
- **G-code generation**: Writer functionality, cooling, lift/unlift
- **Slicing algorithms**: Layer generation, infill patterns
- **Print mechanics**: Flow calculations, extrusion, support material
- **Model processing**: Print objects, skirt/brim generation

### sla_print Tests
Stereolithography specific tests:
- **SLA print processing**: Layer curing, support generation
- **Raycast operations**: Light path calculations
- **Test utilities**: SLA-specific helper functions

## Writing New Tests - Best Practices

### File Organization
1. **Naming Convention**: `test_<feature>.cpp` (e.g., `test_geometry.cpp`)
2. **Header Structure**: Include `<catch2/catch_all.hpp>` first, then relevant headers
3. **Namespace Usage**: Use `using namespace Slic3r;` for convenience
4. **File Placement**: Add to appropriate test directory and update CMakeLists.txt

### Test Naming and Structure
```cpp
#include <catch2/catch_all.hpp>
#include "libslic3r/Point.hpp"

using namespace Slic3r;

TEST_CASE("Feature description", "[category_tag]") {
    // Test implementation
}
```

### Tagging System
Use descriptive tags for test categorization:
- `[Geometry]` - Geometric operations and calculations
- `[GCodeWriter]` - G-code generation functionality  
- `[Config]` - Configuration and settings tests
- `[FileFormat]` - File I/O operations (STL, 3MF, etc.)
- `[Algorithm]` - Core algorithms and processing
- `[Performance]` - Performance benchmarks (if applicable)

## Catch2 Features Guide

### Basic Assertions
```cpp
// Primary assertions - stop test on failure
REQUIRE(expression);
REQUIRE_FALSE(expression);

// Continuing assertions - continue test after failure  
CHECK(expression);
CHECK_FALSE(expression);

// Non-failing checks - record result but don't fail test
CHECK_NOFAIL(expression);  // Useful for assumptions that might be violated
```

### Exception Testing
```cpp
// Verify no exception is thrown
REQUIRE_NOTHROW(function_call());

// Verify any exception is thrown
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());

// Verify specific exception type
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(function_call(), SpecificException);

// Verify exception message
REQUIRE_THROWS_WITH(function_call(), "Expected error message");

// Verify exception with matchers (for partial matching)
REQUIRE_THROWS_MATCHES(function_call(), SpecificException, 
                       Catch::Matchers::Message("contains this"));
```

### Complex Assertions with Matchers
```cpp
#include <catch2/matchers/catch_matchers.hpp>

// String matchers
using Catch::Matchers::StartsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::EndsWith;
using Catch::Matchers::ContainsSubstring;
using Catch::Matchers::Equals;
using Catch::Matchers::Matches;  // Regex matching

REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, StartsWith("Expected prefix"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, ContainsSubstring("middle part"));
REQUIRE_THAT(result_string, Matches(".*pattern.*"));

// Floating point matchers - ALWAYS use these instead of Approx!
using Catch::Matchers::WithinAbs;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinRel;
using Catch::Matchers::WithinULP;

REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinAbs(expected, 0.001));     // Absolute tolerance
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinRel(expected, 0.01));      // Relative tolerance (1%)
REQUIRE_THAT(float_value, WithinULP(expected, 4));         // ULP difference (requires IEEE-754)

// Combining matchers
REQUIRE_THAT(value, WithinRel(expected, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));
```

### Sections for Test Organization
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Complex feature testing", "[Feature]") {
    // Common setup code
    SomeObject obj;
    
    SECTION("First scenario") {
        // Specific test case
        REQUIRE(obj.method1() == expected_value);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second scenario") {
        // Another test case with same setup
        REQUIRE(obj.method2() == other_expected);
    }
}
```

### BDD-Style Tests
Use for complex scenarios and user story testing:

> **Note**: BDD macros are aliases for TEST_CASE and SECTION with prefixed names
```cpp
SCENARIO("User performs complex operation", "[UserStory]") {
    GIVEN("A specific setup condition") {
        GCodeWriter writer;
        // Setup code
        
        WHEN("User performs action") {
            auto result = writer.some_operation();
            
            THEN("Expected outcome occurs") {
                REQUIRE(result.size() > 0);
                
                AND_WHEN("Follow-up action occurs") {
                    auto next_result = writer.next_operation();
                    
                    THEN("Final outcome is correct") {
                        REQUIRE(next_result == expected);
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
```

### Data Generators for Parameterized Tests
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Function works with various inputs", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto test_value = GENERATE(1, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13);
    
    REQUIRE(is_odd(test_value));
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Range-based generators
TEST_CASE("Range testing", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto i = GENERATE(range(1, 10));  // 1 to 9
    REQUIRE(process_value(i) > i);
}

// Using variables in generators (requires GENERATE_COPY or GENERATE_REF)
TEST_CASE("Generator with variables", "[Algorithm]") {
    std::vector<int> values = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
    auto test_value = GENERATE_REF(from_range(values));  // Use GENERATE_REF for references
    
    REQUIRE(test_value > 0);
}

// Custom generators
TEST_CASE("Random values", "[Algorithm]") {
    auto random_int = GENERATE(take(100, random(-1000, 1000)));  // 100 random values
    REQUIRE(process_random_value(random_int));
}
```

### Test Fixtures
```cpp
class GeometryFixture {
public:
    Point origin{0, 0};
    Point unit_x{1, 0};
    Point unit_y{0, 1};
    
    mutable double tolerance = EPSILON;  // Use mutable for data that might change
};

// Standard fixture - new instance per test run
TEST_CASE_METHOD(GeometryFixture, "Point operations", "[Geometry]") {
    REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_x) == 1.0);
}

// Persistent fixture - single instance for entire test case (v3.2.0+)
TEST_CASE_PERSISTENT_FIXTURE(GeometryFixture, "Persistent operations", "[Geometry]") {
    static int call_count = 0;
    ++call_count;
    INFO("This fixture persists across sections, call: " << call_count);
    
    SECTION("First section") {
        REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_x) == 1.0);
    }
    
    SECTION("Second section") {
        REQUIRE(origin.distance_to(unit_y) == 1.0);
        // call_count will be 2 here with persistent fixture
    }
}

// Template fixtures for type-parameterized tests
template<typename T>
class NumericFixture {
public:
    T zero = T{0};
    T one = T{1};
};

TEMPLATE_TEST_CASE_METHOD(NumericFixture, "Numeric operations", "[Template]", int, float, double) {
    REQUIRE(TestType{} == this->zero);
    REQUIRE(TestType{1} == this->one);
}
```

### Advanced Testing Features

#### Logging and Information Macros
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Advanced logging", "[Logging]") {
    INFO("This info persists until end of scope");
    
    SECTION("Section A") {
        INFO("Section A specific info");
        CAPTURE(some_variable, another_var);  // Captures variable names and values
        CHECK(some_condition);
    }
    
    SECTION("Section B") {
        UNSCOPED_INFO("This survives beyond its scope");  // v2.7.0+
        CHECK(other_condition);
    }
}

// Warning and explicit control
TEST_CASE("Explicit test control", "[Control]") {
    WARN("This warns but doesn't fail the test");
    
    if (precondition_not_met) {
        SKIP("Reason");  // Marks the test as skipped (v3.3.0+, available)
        return;
    }
    
    if (critical_failure) {
        FAIL("Critical condition failed");  // Fails and stops test
    }
    
    SUCCEED("Reached successful completion");  // Explicit success marker
}
```

#### Static Assertions (Compile-time Testing)
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Compile-time checks", "[Static]") {
    STATIC_REQUIRE(sizeof(int) >= 4);  // Checked at compile time
    STATIC_REQUIRE_FALSE(std::is_void_v<int>);
    
    // For traits and template metaprogramming
    STATIC_CHECK(std::is_trivially_copyable_v<Point>);  // v3.0.1+
}
```

#### Conditional Testing
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Conditional blocks", "[Conditional]") {
    int value = get_test_value();
    
    // These record the expression but don't count as test failures (v3.0.1+)
    CHECKED_IF(value > 0) {
        // This block runs if value > 0
        REQUIRE(value <= 100);
    } CHECKED_ELSE(value > 0) {
        // This block runs if value <= 0  
        REQUIRE(value >= -100);
    }
}
```

#### Benchmarking (v2.9.0+)
```cpp
TEST_CASE("Performance testing", "[Benchmark]") {
    // Simple benchmarking
    BENCHMARK("Algorithm performance") {
        return expensive_algorithm();
    };
    
    // Advanced benchmarking with setup
    BENCHMARK_ADVANCED("Advanced benchmark")(Catch::Benchmark::Chronometer meter) {
        std::vector<int> data = setup_test_data();  // Setup not measured
        
        meter.measure([&] { 
            return process_data(data);  // Only this is measured
        });
    };

## Common Pitfalls and Solutions

### Floating-Point Comparisons

> **CRITICAL**: Never use Approx - it's deprecated due to asymmetry and other issues

❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == expected_volume);           // Exact equality
REQUIRE(calculated_volume == Catch::Approx(expected));   // Deprecated! Asymmetric!
```

✅ **Correct**: Always use floating point matchers
```cpp
// Absolute tolerance - good when values are near zero
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinAbs(expected_volume, 0.001));

// Relative tolerance - good for values with different magnitudes
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.01));  // 1% tolerance

// ULP (Units in Last Place) - most precise, requires IEEE-754
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, WithinULP(expected_volume, 4));

// Combined approach - relative OR absolute
REQUIRE_THAT(calculated_volume, 
    WithinRel(expected_volume, 0.001) || WithinAbs(0.0, 0.000001));

// Precision control for output
Catch::StringMaker<double>::precision = 15;  // Show more decimal places
```

### Why Approx is Problematic:
- **Asymmetric**: `Approx(10).epsilon(0.1) != 11.1` but `Approx(11.1).epsilon(0.1) == 10`
- **Double-only**: All computation done in `double`, causes issues with `float` inputs  
- **Default behavior**: Only uses relative comparison, so `Approx(0) == X` only works for `X == 0`

### Path Handling
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
std::string path = TEST_DATA_DIR + "/model.obj";  // May have path separator issues
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
std::string path = std::string(TEST_DATA_DIR) + "/model.obj";
// or use boost::filesystem for complex path operations
```

### Exception Testing
❌ **Incorrect**:
```cpp
bool threw_exception = false;
try {
    risky_function();
} catch (...) {
    threw_exception = true;
}
REQUIRE(threw_exception);
```

✅ **Correct**:
```cpp
REQUIRE_THROWS(risky_function());
// or for specific exceptions
REQUIRE_THROWS_AS(risky_function(), SpecificException);
```

### Thread Safety

⚠️ **CRITICAL**: Catch2 assertions are **NOT thread-safe** by default!

> **Note**: Catch2 v3.9.0+ has opt-in thread-safe assertions via `CATCH_CONFIG_EXPERIMENTAL_THREAD_SAFE_ASSERTIONS`. OrcaSlicer is on v3.11.0 but does not enable this flag, so assertions remain non-thread-safe by default.

❌ **Incorrect**: Will cause undefined behavior or crashes
```cpp
std::thread t([&]() {
    REQUIRE(threaded_operation() == expected);  // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
    CHECK(other_operation());                   // NOT THREAD-SAFE!
});
```

✅ **Correct**: Collect results, assert on main thread
```cpp
std::atomic<bool> success{false};
std::atomic<int> error_count{0};

std::thread t([&]() {
    // Do work in thread, collect results
    bool result1 = (threaded_operation() == expected);
    bool result2 = other_operation();
    
    if (result1 && result2) {
        success = true;
    } else {
        error_count++;
    }
});

t.join();

// Assert results on main thread
REQUIRE(success);
REQUIRE(error_count == 0);
```

#### Thread Safety Rules:
- **REQUIRE family**: Would terminate process in spawned threads (throws exception with no try-catch)
- **CHECK family**: Not thread-safe, can corrupt internal state
- **SKIP, FAIL, SUCCEED**: Not thread-safe even with v3 thread-safe assertions
- **Message macros**: INFO, CAPTURE, WARN - not thread-safe
- **STATIC_REQUIRE/CHECK**: Not thread-safe (relies on runtime registration)
